comments.why_zh: 关于 Python 语义中根本问题的精彩演讲。
comments.quote_zh: 下面是著名的 Python Flask 库作者的一个精彩演讲
comments.text_zh: 正如其他人提到的，Python 确实有 JIT 编译器。问题在于，有 JIT 并不能解决问题。PyPy 的性能常常比 Julia 落后 10 倍，而 Numba、PyTorch（PyTorch 的人不得不自己构建 Python JIT 编译器，天哪！）等项目，其适用范围永远会比 Julia 这样的项目更受限，因为 Python 的语义本身就让许多优化无法实现。下面是著名的 Python Flask 库作者的一个精彩演讲：[VIDEO] 他在其中讨论了 Python 语义的根本问题。如果你修复这些问题，最终会把 Python 改得面目全非，以至于它实际上会变成一门新语言。普通的 CPython 3._ 代码肯定无法与之兼容。
comments.text: As others have mentioned, Python does have JIT compilers. The problem is that havign a JIT doesn't solve the problem. PyPy is often a factor of 10 behind julia performance and projects like Numba, PyTorch (the PyTorch people had to build their own Python JIT compiler yikes!), etc. will always have a more restricted scope than a project like Julia because Python's very semantics make many optimizations impossible. Here's a great talk from the author of the famous Flask library in Python: [VIDEO] where he discusses the fundamental problems with Python's semantics. If you fix these problems, you will end up changing Python so fundamentaly that you'll really have a new language. Generic CPython 3._ code will certainly not be compatible with it.

comments.author: arc776
comments.why_zh: 说明 Python 优化的局限。
comments.quote_zh: 我强烈推荐这里发布的两个视频
comments.text_zh: 正如 OP 所说：> 可变解释器帧、全局解释器锁、共享全局状态、类型槽。除此之外，Python 极其动态，不跑一遍代码就无法保证任何事情。因此才需要 JIT 来提升性能，而这又带来启动慢和复杂度增加。即便有 JIT，由于上述问题以及整体的动态性，Python 就是不够快。它可以被优化，而且肯定有一些令人印象深刻的尝试。但我不认为纯 Python 会被称为“快”，因为这些东西必然会碍事。我强烈推荐这里发布的两个视频，它们更详细地说明了为什么优化能走多远是有限制的：[VIDEO] [LINK]
comments.text: As the OP states: > mutable interpreter frames, global interpreter locks, shared global state, type slots On top of this, Python is extremely dynamic and nothing can be assured without running through the code. So this leads to needing JITs to improve performance which then give a slow start up time and increased complexity. Even with JIT, Python is just not fast thanks to the above issues and it's overall dynamism. It can be optimised and for sure there's some impressive attempts at doing so. However I don't think pure Python will ever be considered "fast" as these things necessarily get in the way. I highly recommend the two videos posted here that go into more detail as to why there are limits to how far optimisation can go: [VIDEO] [LINK]

comments.author: haberman
comments.why_zh: 展示 Python 的 add 操作语义实际上有多复杂。
comments.quote_zh: 这个出色的演讲描述了“add”操作的语义比通常描述的要复杂得多。
comments.text_zh: 由于复杂的语言语义，Python 很难优化。这个出色的演讲描述了“add”操作的语义比通常描述的要复杂得多。a+b 并不只是 a.__add__(b)，你必须阅读 200 多行 CPython 解释器代码才能完全弄清其语义：[VIDEO] 不是说不可能，但相比优化那些语义更规整的语言，这更像是一场逆风战。Python 还受限于它的 C API，这个 API 级别非常低，向 C 扩展暴露了大量实现细节。改变 API 可以提升性能，但也会让 Python 与庞大的 C 扩展生态不兼容。我有时希望 Python 定义一个新的 C API，暴露的东西少得多，并开始向新 API 的长期迁移，这样最终解释器受到的约束会少一些。这会是一次大规模迁移，但与 Python 2 -> 3 不同，它不会影响日常用户，只会影响扩展作者。我不知道这是否会发生，但人总可以做梦。
comments.text: Python is difficult to optimize due to complex language semantics. This excellent talk describes how the semantics of the "add" operation are much more complex than generally described. a+b is not just a.__add__(b), you have to read 200+ lines of CPython interpreter code to fully resolve its semantics: [VIDEO] Not saying it's impossible, but it's more of an uphill battle than optimizing other languages that have more regular semantics. Python is also constrained by its C API, which is a very low-level and exposes a lot of implementation details to C extensions. Changing the API could improve performance but it would also make Python incompatible with a large ecosystem of C extensions. I sometimes wish for Python to define a new C API that exposes far less, and to begin a long-term migration towards the new API so that eventually the interpreter would be less constrained. It would be a large migration, but unlike Python 2 -> 3 it wouldn't affect everyday users, only extension authors. I don't know if it will ever happen, but a person can dream.

comments.author: ssivark
comments.story_title: How Numba and Cython speed up Python code
comments.why_zh: 为什么 Python 的设计会阻碍性能优化。
comments.quote_zh: 讲为什么 Python 的设计从根本上对性能优化不友好
comments.text_zh: 大多数高性能 Python 库都不是那样写的，核心例程干脆用 C 写，这是有原因的。布丁好不好，吃了才知道！看看 Armin Ronacher（Flask 的作者）的这个演讲，讲为什么 Python 的设计从根本上对性能优化不友好：[VIDEO] Julia 从一开始就是为了避免若干这类问题而设计的。看看这个讨论：[LINK] 如果你的领域属于数值与科学计算，写 Julia 和写 Python 一样轻松，代码自动就能跑得大致和 C 一样快。如果你习惯写 numpy，你可以很快上手 Julia，也许几个小时就能适应略有不同的语法和有用库的名字。
comments.text: There's a reason most high-performance Python libraries are not written that way, and core routines are just written in C instead. Proof of the pudding is in the eating! See this talk by Armin Ronacher (creator of Flask) on why the design of python makes it fundamentally unfriendly to performance optimizations: [VIDEO] Julia has be designed ground up to avoid several such problems. See this discussion: [LINK] If your domain falls under the umbrella of numerical and scientific computing, writing Julia is as painless as writing python, with code that automatically runs roughly as fast as C. If you're used to writing numpy, you can hit the ground running in Julia, with maybe a few hours to become comfortable with the slightly different syntax and the names of useful libraries.

comments.text_zh: Python 的成功完全是应得的。它花了这么久才走到今天（Python 都快 30 岁了！），这表明其中投入了巨大的努力，也应该给所有致力于构建下一代语言的人以鼓舞。既然这个论坛里很可能有一些着眼未来的人，我觉得 Python 老将 Armin Ronacher 的两个演讲很有意思 [1, 2]。看那个演讲让我开始想，我是否应该把它放在“Worse is better”的语境下来思考。话虽如此，Python 的运行时内省是一个杀手级特性，对于相对较新的编程者来说，很难解释这种能力感有多让人振奋。[1]：How Python was Shaped by leaky Internals -- [VIDEO] [2]：A Python for Future Generations -- [LINK]
comments.text: Python's success is richly deserved. The fact that it has been a long time coming (Python is almost 30 years old!) is an indication of the amount of sheer effort involved, and should give heart for all those working on building up the next generation of languages. Since this forum is likely to have some folks looking towards the future, I found interesting a couple of talks by Python veteran Armin Ronacher [1, 2]. Watching that presentation makes me wonder whether I should think of this in the context of "Worse is better". That said, Python's runtime introspection is such a killer feature that it's difficult to explain how empowering it feels for someone who is relatively new to programming. [1]: How Python was Shaped by leaky Internals -- [VIDEO] [2]: A Python for Future Generations -- [LINK]
